content: The Peruvian Torch cactus, scientifically known as Trichocereus peruvianus, is a rapidly growing columnar cactus that is indigenous to the western slopes of the Andes in Peru. It is also occasionally referred to as the Peruvian Fence Post. This plant exhibits a bluish-green coloration with frosted stems and features 6 to 8 broad, rounded ribs. It produces large, white flowers. The cactus can reach a height of up to 7 meters, with stems that can grow up to 20 centimeters in diameter. Initially, the plant grows fully erect, but over time, it may arch over or even become prostrate. A short-spined variant of this cactus exists, which closely resembles its relative, the San Pedro cactus. This similarity has led to frequent misidentifications, with plants being sold under incorrect names, either as Peruvian Torch or San Pedro. The presence of local variations and hybrids, both cultivated and naturally occurring, further complicates accurate identification. Chemistry The Peruvian Torch cactus contains several psychoactive alkaloids, most notably mescaline, a well-studied compound. The mescaline content in this cactus is higher than that found in the San Pedro cactus, although it is not as high as in peyote, contrary to some incorrect claims. Usage Historically, the Peruvian Torch cactus has been utilized by various religious and spiritual groups, including shamans and Native Americans, for its psychoactive properties.
